name: ldapsearch
one_line: query an LDAP directory (such as Active Directory)
plain: `ldapsearch` asks an LDAP server questions. LDAP is the directory service behind Active Directory: it holds users, groups, computers and policies. The shape is `ldapsearch -H ldap://SERVER -x -b BASE FILTER ATTRIBUTES`.

Two ideas: the BASE is where in the directory tree you start (for example `dc=corp,dc=local`), and the FILTER says what to find (`(objectClass=user)`). Many servers allow an anonymous bind (no password) to read a little: a classic first enumeration step in a lab.
when: List the naming contexts of a domain controller.
Enumerate users, groups and computers with valid credentials.
Find descriptions or notes that contain a password (a common CTF clue).
Check whether anonymous access is allowed.

examples.title: Find the base DN
examples.explain: -x is simple authentication (no SASL), -s base asks only about the root entry. namingContexts shows the base names to use next.

examples.title: Anonymous search
examples.explain: Tries to read everything without a password. Often refused, sometimes a few entries come back.

examples.title: List users
examples.explain: -D is the account, -w the password. The final words are attributes to show: names and descriptions (descriptions sometimes hold passwords).

examples.title: Clean output
examples.explain: -LLL removes comments and version lines, leaving tidy entries you can parse.

examples.title: One user
examples.explain: -W asks for the password without putting it in your shell history.

examples.title: Groups and members
examples.explain: (&(A)(B)) means A and B. This lists who is in Domain Admins.

examples.title: Encrypted connection
examples.explain: ldaps:// uses TLS; -ZZ on a plain ldap:// URL starts TLS and fails if it cannot.

options.plain: Password on the command line / prompt / from a file.
options.use: Prefer -W or -y: -w shows in the process list.

options.plain: Search extension, such as paged results (pr=1000).
Run a search for each line of a file.
Show what would be done without doing it.
The search filter, for example (objectClass=user) or (&(a=1)(b=2)).

mistakes: Using the wrong base DN: read namingContexts first.
Putting a password with -w in the shell history: use -W.
Forgetting the quotes around a filter, so the shell mangles the parentheses.
Expecting anonymous binds to work on modern servers: most refuse them.
try: Ask a lab domain controller for its namingContexts.
List sAMAccountName for every user and read the descriptions.
Find the members of a privileged group.
Compare the result with BloodHound's view of the same domain.
